titles.title: Metate (grinding stone) in the form of a feline

texts.textentryhtml:
By June 1961, Stanley J. Seeger, Jr. (1930-2011), Class of 1952 [1]; gift to Mr. and Mrs. Patrick J. Kelleher [2]; 1971, gift of Mr. and Mrs. Patrick J. Kelleher to the Princeton University Art Museum.

Notes:
[1] Included in Patrick J. Kelleher, The Stanley J. Seeger Jr. Collection on Special Exhibition During June 1961 (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Art Museum, 1961), fig. 141, ill.
[2] According to note on the Princeton University Art Museum accession card.

Ferocious felines inspired ancient Central Americans just as they do Princeton Tigers today. With muscular bodies, sharp claws, and a deadly bite, cats stealthily track prey with silent footsteps, their reflective eyes shining in the night. Lightning-fast on the ground and adept at maneuvering through treetops as well as underwater, they are masters of three realms (in, on, and above the earth). Four species of big cats with spotted pelts are native to Central America: the jaguar, ocelot, margay, and oncilla, from largest to smallest. The size and head shape on this metate (“grinding stone” in Hispanicized Nahuatl) resemble those of an ocelot. With stone hand tools, Native artists laboriously transformed large volcanic boulders into bodies of animals, rendering their distinctive markings with geometric bands of carving surrounding a large concave surface. Used to process foods like cassava and yucca tubers, as well as medicine, pigments, and other materials, the metate may also have served as a seat.

Alanna Radlo-Dzur, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Department of Art and Archaeology, Princeton University
